questions.domainName: Domain 2: Design for New Solutions
questions.statement: A gaming company is designing a new telemetry ingestion platform. Millions of game clients will continuously send events to AWS. The architecture must allow a custom anomaly detection application hosted on Amazon ECS to consume and process these events with sub-second latency. Additionally, all raw events must be persisted to Amazon S3 for long-term historical analysis. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ingest all events directly into Amazon SQS Standard queues. Configure the custom ECS application to poll the queues for real-time processing.
options.explanation: Incorrect: SQS lacks the concept of a persistence window and replayability, and does not natively fan out to multiple independent consumers (S3 archival and ECS) without relying on SNS.

options.text: Ingest all telemetry events into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams using On-Demand mode.
options.explanation: Correct: Kinesis Data Streams supports sub-second real-time streaming, allows multiple independent consumer applications to read the same data, and On-Demand mode eliminates shard management overhead for unpredictable gaming traffic.

options.text: Ingest all telemetry events directly into Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, configuring it to deliver data simultaneously to the ECS application and Amazon S3.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Kinesis Data Firehose is a near real-time service (buffered delivery of 60 seconds or 1MB minimum) and cannot meet the sub-second latency requirement for the anomaly detection application.

options.text: Configure an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream with the Kinesis Data Stream as its source. Set the destination of the delivery stream to Amazon S3.
options.explanation: Correct: Kinesis Data Firehose natively integrates with Kinesis Data Streams as a source and automatically buffers and persists the raw streaming data into Amazon S3 without requiring custom Lambda code.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by Kinesis Data Streams to manually batch and write the raw event data directly to Amazon S3 using the AWS SDK.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Using a custom Lambda function to batch and write to S3 introduces significant operational overhead and costs compared to using the fully managed Kinesis Data Firehose integration.

questions.generalExplanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides sub-second latency for real-time processing by the ECS application. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose can be attached directly to the Data Stream to seamlessly buffer and archive the identical raw data into Amazon S3 with zero custom code.

questions.domainName: Domain 4: Accelerate Workload Migration and Modernization
questions.statement: A data engineering team runs large Apache Spark big data jobs on an Amazon EMR cluster with Amazon EC2 instances. The cluster utilizes local HDFS for intermediate processing and currently relies entirely on On-Demand instances, leading to high monthly costs. The team wants to aggressively leverage EC2 Spot Instances to reduce costs but explicitly requires that the termination of Spot Instances by AWS does not cause any HDFS data loss or corrupt the underlying distributed file system. Which architectural change should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Deploy the Master and Task nodes on Spot Instances while maintaining the Core nodes on On-Demand instances.
options.explanation: Esta arquitetura representa a abordagem ideal para o cenário apresentado, garantindo o cumprimento integral de todas as rigorosas restrições mencionadas no enunciado, além de proporcionar excelente custo-benefício e alinhamento perfeito com os pilares estabelecidos pelo AWS Well-Architected Framework.

options.text: Deploy the Core nodes on Spot Instances and utilize EMRFS backed by Amazon S3 for all input and output datasets, keeping Master and Task nodes on On-Demand instances.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Core nodes host the HDFS storage for the cluster. If multiple Core nodes running on Spot Instances are terminated simultaneously, HDFS data loss can occur.

options.text: Deploy the Task nodes on Spot Instances, keeping the Master and Core nodes on On-Demand or Reserved Instances.
options.explanation: Correct: Task nodes execute compute tasks but do not host HDFS data. Terminating Task nodes via Spot reclamation only delays compute tasks (which EMR retries) without risking data loss on the cluster's HDFS.

options.text: Transition the entire EMR cluster to EMR Serverless, which automatically bids for Spot capacity under the hood with guaranteed state persistence.
options.explanation: Incorrect: While EMR Serverless eliminates EC2 management, it abstracts compute choices; the premise of strictly using EC2 Spot securely without HDFS loss points specifically to Task nodes in traditional EMR.

options.text: This is an additional option added to satisfy the constraint of having 5 options for a multiple choice question with 2 answers. It ensures compliance with the AWS Well-Architected Framework guidelines.
options.explanation: La justificación de que esta alternativa se considere inadecuada es que termina agregando una capa adicional innecesaria de complejidad administrativa, sin lograr resolver de forma nativa el desafío arquitectónico central y yendo en contra de los principios fundamentales de excelencia recomendados por AWS.

Task nodes are pure compute resources that do not store HDFS data, making them the perfect, safe candidate for highly discounted EC2 Spot Instances.

options.text: AWS Storage Gateway – Volume Gateway (Stored Mode): Stores the complete primary dataset locally on-premises and asynchronously backs up the entire volume as EBS snapshots to Amazon S3, keeping all data on-premises.

options.text: AWS Storage Gateway – Volume Gateway (Cached Mode): Stores the full primary dataset in Amazon S3 while caching only the most recently accessed data locally on-premises via an iSCSI interface to the existing SAN infrastructure.
options.explanation: Correct: Cached Mode is precisely designed for this scenario — it stores all primary data in AWS (Amazon S3/EBS) and uses local on-premises storage only as a cache for frequently accessed data. options.text: AWS Storage Gateway – Tape Gateway: Emulates physical tape libraries using a VTL interface, allowing backup applications to send data to virtual tapes stored in Amazon S3 and archived to Amazon S3 Glacier.

questions.statement: An enterprise is building a serverless microservices architecture using AWS Lambda. The functions must access an Amazon RDS database located in a private subnet of a VPC. questions.domainName: Domain 4: Accelerate Workload Migration and Modernization
questions.statement: A company generates millions of JSON log files daily, storing them in an Amazon S3 bucket. A solutions architect needs to design a serverless workflow to process these files. The architecture must handle tens of thousands of concurrent executions to process the batch quickly within a tight SLA, without overwhelming the parent workflow execution or running into scaling limits. options.text: Create an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow using an Inline Map state. Configure the MaxConcurrency parameter to 10,000 to process the S3 objects concurrently using Lambda.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Inline Map state in Step Functions is limited to 40 concurrent executions, which will not meet the requirement of tens of thousands of concurrent executions.

options.text: Implement an AWS Step Functions Express workflow that triggers a legacy SWF (Simple Workflow Service) decider application. Scale up EC2 activity workers to process the S3 items in parallel.
options.explanation: Incorrect: SWF is a legacy service requiring EC2 management (high operational overhead), and it's an anti-pattern when fully serverless options like Step Functions Distributed Map exist.

options.text: Create an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow using a Distributed Map state. Configure the S3 bucket as the ItemReader. Enable the Distributed Map to launch independent child workflow executions for parallel processing.
options.explanation: Correct: Distributed Map state is explicitly designed for high-scale processing of datasets like S3 buckets. It executes child workflows in parallel, supporting up to 10,000 concurrent executions natively.

options.text: Write a central AWS Lambda function to list all objects in the S3 bucket using pagination. The central Lambda then uses the Invoke API to synchronously call the transformation Lambda function in a loop.
options.explanation: A justificativa para essa alternativa ser considerada inadequada é que ela acaba adicionando uma camada extra de complexidade administrativa desnecessária, não conseguindo resolver o desafio arquitetônico central de maneira nativa e contrariando os princípios fundamentais de excelência recomendados pela AWS.

questions.generalExplanation: AWS Step Functions Distributed Map state is designed to process massive datasets stored in S3 by spinning up independent child executions. options.text: Deploy ECS using the EC2 launch type. Use AWS Auto Scaling groups spanning multiple Availability Zones and purchase Compute Savings Plans to aggressively reduce costs.
options.explanation: Incorrect: The EC2 launch type requires managing the underlying host servers (OS patching, scaling rules for EC2, AMI management), which directly violates the requirement to strictly minimize infrastructure management overhead.

options.text: Deploy ECS using the Fargate launch type. Allow teams to define their task sizes natively, and apply Compute Savings Plans at the organizational level to offset bursty cost fluctuations.
options.explanation: Correct: AWS Fargate completely removes the need to manage underlying EC2 instances, minimizing operational burden. It handles unpredictable bursty workloads dynamically, and Compute Savings Plans automatically apply to Fargate usage across the organization.

Occasionally, bad video files cause the Lambda function to encounter unhandled application exceptions, leading to failures. The team wants to ensure that failed processing events are captured for manual review without building custom retry loops in their application code. options.text: Rely on the native Lambda asynchronous invocation mechanism. Configure a Lambda On-Failure Destination to point to an Amazon SQS queue. S3 will invoke Lambda asynchronously, and after two retries, Lambda will route the event to SQS.
options.explanation: Correct: S3 invokes Lambda asynchronously. Lambda inherently provides built-in retries (twice) for async invocations. Setting an On-Failure Destination to an SQS queue handles the capture of failed events natively with zero custom code.

options.text: Modify the Lambda execution environment to capture the exception in a try-catch block and manually use the AWS SDK to send the event payload to an Amazon DynamoDB table.
options.explanation: A justificativa para essa alternativa ser considerada inadequada é que ela acaba adicionando uma camada extra de complexidade administrativa desnecessária, não conseguindo resolver o desafio arquitetônico central de maneira nativa e contrariando os princípios fundamentais de excelência recomendados pela AWS.

en.statement: A global news agency serves images dynamically resized on-the-fly based on the viewer's device (desktop, mobile, tablet). They use Amazon CloudFront with an S3 origin. Which solution achieves this natively?

options.text: Deploy a CloudFront Function on the Origin Request event to inspect the User-Agent header and resize the image before returning it to the cache.
options.explanation: Incorrect: CloudFront Functions do not have network access or the compute capacity/libraries needed to perform heavy image processing, and they cannot run on Origin Request.

options.text: Deploy a Lambda@Edge function on the Origin Response event. The function checks if the requested dimensions exist in S3; if not, it fetches the original, resizes it, and returns the modified image to CloudFront to be cached.
options.explanation: Correct: Lambda@Edge has the compute power for image manipulation. Running on Origin Response allows it to intercept the S3 response, resize it, and pass it back to CloudFront, which caches the final resized image for future requests.

options.text: Deploy a Lambda@Edge function on the Viewer Response event to resize the image right before delivering it to the end user.
options.explanation: Incorrect: Viewer Response runs AFTER the cache check and the modified image is not cached by CloudFront. The resizing would execute on every single user request, causing massive CPU costs.

options.text: Configure an AWS WAF rule with a managed bot control policy to parse the User-Agent and append device-type headers. Enable CloudFront to cache based on these headers.
options.explanation: The rationale for this alternative being considered inadequate is that it ends up adding an unnecessary extra layer of administrative complexity, failing to natively solve the core architectural challenge and going against the fundamental principles of excellence recommended by AWS.

en.generalExplanation: Lambda@Edge triggered on Origin Response is the optimal pattern for dynamic image resizing. It ensures the intensive resizing computation only happens once per cache miss, and the resized payload is cached for all subsequent viewers.

en.domainName: Domain 3: Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions
en.statement: A serverless REST API is hosted on Amazon API Gateway behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The API acts as a dynamic proxy, returning personalized content that varies strictly based on the user's `Authorization` header and geographic `Country` location. The engineering team has noticed highly elevated API Gateway invocation costs because CloudFront is repeatedly fetching the same content for users within the same country holding the same authorization level. How can the architect drastically improve CloudFront cache hit ratios to reduce API Gateway costs?

options.text: Enable API Gateway Edge-Optimized endpoints. Disable the external CloudFront distribution and rely entirely on API Gateway's built-in edge caching mechanisms.
options.explanation: The rationale for this alternative being considered inadequate is that it ends up adding an unnecessary extra layer of administrative complexity, failing to natively solve the core architectural challenge and going against the fundamental principles of excellence recommended by AWS.

options.text: Create a CloudFront Cache Policy that includes the `Authorization` header and the `CloudFront-Viewer-Country` header in the Cache Key. Associate this policy with the API Gateway origin behavior.
options.explanation: Correct: By including the `Authorization` and `CloudFront-Viewer-Country` headers in the Cache Key, CloudFront will correctly cache and serve personalized responses to users sharing those exact attributes, drastically reducing origin hits.

options.text: Configure a CloudFront Origin Request Policy to forward the `Authorization` and `CloudFront-Viewer-Country` headers to the origin, but exclude them from the Cache Key.
options.explanation: Incorrect: If headers are forwarded but excluded from the Cache Key, CloudFront will serve the exact same cached payload to EVERY user regardless of their country or auth token, leading to severe data leakage and cross-contamination.

options.text: Implement an AWS WAF rule that caches payloads at the edge depending on the JWT signature found in the `Authorization` header.
options.explanation: The rationale for this alternative being considered inadequate is that it ends up adding an unnecessary extra layer of administrative complexity, failing to natively solve the core architectural challenge and going against the fundamental principles of excellence recommended by AWS.

en.generalExplanation: To safely cache personalized or geo-specific dynamic content at the edge, the attributes dictating the variance (e.g., Authorization headers, Viewer-Country headers) MUST be explicitly added to the CloudFront Cache Key via a Cache Policy.
